Hello middle_path, sounds like a rough situation, here is what I can offer:

----Like Vito Mass said, under no circumstances can you default on or miss payments, this literally has to be the dead last option with no other way out. Defaulting on a loan is going to have disastrous financial consequences down the road such as being sent to collections (which will be a pain to deal with not to mention the tremendous fees they will add on that you are legally responsible for), possible wage garnishes, and a whole mountain of other trouble.

----Also, I crunched the numbers into a loan calculator online and gathered a few more important numbers you left out, repayment period and total money paid. Here is what I found regarding those numbers on your wife's loans: (here is websites if you want to double check https://www.calcxml.com/calculators/pay-off-loan?skn=#results and http://www.practicalmoneyskills.com/calculators/calculate/howMuchWillMyLoanCost.php?calcCategory=debt)

  • 17,473 - 10.5% - 179.81 - 18.2 years - 37,147 total
  • 13,442 - 6.25% - 103.25 - 18.3 years - 22,527 total
  • 7,998 - 9.62% - 171.05 - 4.9 years - 10,063 total
  • 25,036 - 9.72% - 278.82 - 13.5 years - 44,911 total
  • 26,659 - 7.75% - 266.13 - 13.5 years - 43,041 total
  • 17,477 - 5% - 190.92 - 9.7 years - 22,054 total
  • 4,014 - 6.8% - 52.66 - 8.4 years - 5,270 total

Please edit your original post to include these numbers as they are very important factors to consider.

From those numbers you should contact the 3 loans that are below 10 years and tell them you want to renegotiate them to a 15 or 20 year (or 10 for that 5 year loan) repayment option. Make sure when you speak to them make it abundantly clear you have every intention of fully paying the loans but you have a child on the way and with your current income will be IMPOSSIBLE to make the current rate of payments. You are not reaching out to them out of convenience but necessity and your desire to meet your financial obligation. Make sure to you find the appropriate balance between complaining about your debt and presenting a clear and detailed summary of your finances and how this is necessary for both you and them.

More than anything these companies want to get paid so you MUST have numbers to present to them that show this is to their benefit as much as yours. The numbers are important as it will also demonstrate to them that you are smart with planning this out and it will instill more faith in them of you.

As an example, let's use your 7998 loan.
You are paying a whopping 171.05 monthly rate on a low balance loan because of the short repayment period. If you can get them to agree to a 15 year loan payment that same monthly payment is reduced to $84 per month. Now they will probably not agree to something that is break even like that but if you can get them agree to 90 or 100 per month for 15 years you nearly cut your payment in half but at the same time they will see an extra $2800 when the loan is paid off. I admit I am not an expert at negotiating but you see what I am getting at right? Focus on showing the benefit to them about letting you make lower monthly payments for a larger payout on their end AND that you will no longer have to default on the loan.

I can help you crunch some of the other numbers if you need help but try on your own googling various loan repayment calculators and see what you come up with. Of course, please feel free to ask if you need help.

Remember, when you speak to them they are not your friends, but not your enemies either. They are someone who can hopefully see the value that both of you get out of restructuring your loans. You defaulting on your loans is just as bad for them as it is for you.

----Do NOT pay off loans early simply because you can. Your income will most likely increase as you get further in your careers and make your debt much more manageable. Make the minimum payments and go through hell and high water to start setting money aside for savings. Even if it is only a little bit do what you can.

I paid off my loans early and regret it tremendously. I am financially sound now but I would much rather have $30000 in the bank in savings as opposed to the $3000 I have now. Paying off my loans early cut my monthly payments in half but in the long run was totally not worth it to blow my savings.

----Like others have mentioned. Focus on working another job (no matter how small) to supplement your income. Make sure you do not burn out as you have a kid on the way and absolutely will want time with him/her but at the same time you need to make sure you kid won't have to have problems with your financial issues.

----Consider welfare or other government resources to help. This doesn't necessarily mean monetary. Some offer free consultation on debt and may offer other resources to help you work through the negotiations and finance calculations. Don't be afraid to reach out if you need help.

Hope this helps and if there is anything else I can answer that may assist please let me know.

I know I'm late to this thread -- I want to comment because I have not only had student debt, but also had unemployment + my wife's business fail + new baby during the great recession years. It sucked. We eventually came out the other side, so it is possible.

GOOD BANK / BAD BANK

When my wife's business failed, her credit, finances, everything, became crap. We realized that we had become somewhat divided where our finances were concerned. I came to think of us as one of those failed big banks -- when they get into financial straits, they often split themselves up, in to a "good bank" that sequesters the good assets, and a "bad bank" that goes into liquidation and write-downs. My wife's accounts were subject to garnishments and other things, and we learned fast that we had to keep our finances separated, and keep t he cash in my accounts. If her accounts were always empty (or very nearly) they couldn't take anything.

This good bank/bad bank separation helped us compartmentalize. Whose "name" such-and-such is in, is largely a legal nitpick. We were married, and already shared everything ... but kept our own separate checking/savings/credit accounts. When it was clear we were going to sequester the bad stuff in her name, we both felt better about having a plan. I would make money and shelter the income, she would watch the baby and work on negotiating with her creditors, and working her way toward an inevitable bankruptcy (she eventually did NOT file, but it was close).

INTEREST RATES

Looking at the details of what you owe, the biggest thing that jumps out at me are your interest rates. I would plot and scheme every possible way to reduce your rates to as close to 0% as possible.

BORROW FROM PETER TO PAY PAUL

People always poo-poo this strategy. However the one time that it is a GOOD strategy is when "Peter" is a nice guy and "Paul" is a goon who wants to break your legs. Well, the lenders charging you 7% and up are breaking your legs right now. There have to be lenders out there where you can consolidate to lower rates. I have consolidated portions of student loans onto 0% or 2% credit cards. I have done the credit-card-balance-transfer game with amounts approaching the $30K that you owe on your student loans. Think outside the box a little and don't give up until you get your interest rates down below 5%, and then try to go to zero. Try LendingTree, try your family, try borrowing from anywhere/anybody to get your interest rates down.

STAY CLOSE TO FAMILY - STAY SANE - IT GETS WORSE

I was the "good bank" in our relationship, but it also meant that it was up to me to do the earning. Unless you have free/unlimited child care from family, your wife's working capacity will greatly diminish for at least the first 3 or possibly 5 years of your child's life. This division of responsibilities can be very tough on your relationship. You'll resent her because you have to constantly work and earn, after all you are the "responsible one who didn't take on all that debt" -- and she'll resent you because her body is a wreck, she has debts and no way to pay them, and she now has a new identity as "mommy". Normal couples with no debt and much better circumstances get ripped apart by these issues. Having a plan and supporting each other will be key to the sanity of both of you.

You simply need to earn as much as possible, and have to continue to grow your income. You already know this. Living in a "remote area" is almost always bad for earnings. As others suggested, you'll have to seriously consider moving to a better area with better paying jobs eventually. Like, maybe when your child is 3 or 4. If you are living with family, or near family, that will be worth a lot of money during your child's first years. It might even allow your wife to return to work quicker. There were many many times when I wished for help after my child was born ... being broke in a far-away city really reduces your options and can put a damper on your mental health.

LOSE THE CAR PAYMENT ASAP

A car payment is sheer insanity for the two of you. If you did the math on the cost of your wife's commute, plus the car payment, time, and gas, her earnings won't look so hot. She'd likely be better off working for less pay at a job that is waking / biking / bus distance from your home (and she might have an easier time keeping/resuming a job like that after the baby comes.) You said you had $3K in savings, and I would say it is worth eliminating 30% of your savings to kill the car payment.

There are a lot of bike-car calculations and I can't really write about it any better than this guy does: the true cost of commuting

LOVE THE SMALL AND SIMPLE LIFE

A great blessing is that kids don't need to cost much. They don't even know what's going on for several years -- all they want is food and warmth and love. Parks are free, walks and bike rides are free, playing with other kids is free. If there's an awesome time to be broke in this world, it's when your kids are little!

Debt or insolvency or general financial troubles befall people for lots of reasons. Decisions don't always pan out, simple as that. During the recession I was mad at myself, mad at my wife, mad at the universe -- I was running out of people and things to be mad at. I can tell you I was extraordinarily jealous of the happy families with little babies, who had jobs, and houses, and support from family members. We were by ourselves, broke, out of work (along with everyone else we knew) looking at bankruptcy, and getting food at the food bank. At times I felt like all the air was being sucked out of the world and I was in some kind of vacuum. All that to say, yeah, I get it. You have some really hard times and dark days ahead, for sure, but eventually time will pass, you and your wife will get back to work and earning, and eventually will make more money than you are now. Working through very tough problems can strengthen your relationship and actually build the foundation of your future family.

Sorry for rambling.

Best of luck to you.
